In #38547, I introduce the notion of two submodules being topological complements to each other, as a predicate Submodule.IsTopCompl. In the API, I add the topological version of docs#Submodule.IsCompl.projection, which I call Submodule.IsTopCompl.projection.

Mimicking what's happening in docs#Submodule.IsCompl.projection, the only explicit argument is a prop (IsCompl in the algebraic case, Submodule.IsTopCompl in the topological case). However, as pointed by @Monica Omar in the review, this has the disadvantage that, as soon as the proof is more than a variable, this gets pretty printed as ⋯.projection. Most importantly, this means that one has no way to know what the kernel and range of the projections are without hovering on the ⋯. This also shows up in the documentation (docs#Submodule.toLinearMap_starProjection_eq_isComplProjection), which is even worse because hovering is useless there.

Monica suggests that, because of this, we should also make the two submodules in docs#Submodule.IsCompl.projection explicit, so that it's always clear which projection we are talking about; this is what's happening in docs#Submodule.linearProjOfIsCompl for example. This makes me a bit sad because I find these explicit parameters are just clutter when writing the code, but I don't have a good idea for a solution.

Would it be possible to make a clever use of the pretty printer here? Two things come to mind:

  • when the proof is relatively short (typically, if it is h.symm), can we teach the pretty printer to display h.symm.projection? Or is proof irrelevance happening too early for this to be possible?
  • when the proof is long, would it be possible to display this as ⋯.projection (ker := _) (rng := _)?

Aside from pretty printers, I find making them explicit parameters also more convenient to use in general. Different from theorem, usage of def items, such as embedding in another def, often requires one to write non-prop parameter first, then construct a proof for the prop.

I received the same review suggestion in the past, amd have been suggesting the same in other PRs since then

Yes, I believe I was the one originating this suggestion, and my reasoning was that proof arguments shouldn't be relied on to decide what a function call does, and also that it prevents authors from mistakenly putting their definition inside a predicate's namespace to leverage dot notation. Eg docs#Finset.cons calls are very readable and I do not wish for the first two arguments to become implicit
Are you claiming that, on top of making the arguments implicit, we should rename docs#Submodule.IsCompl.projection to something like Submodule.projectionOfIsCompl ?
Yes, except I would rename it to Submodule.projection instead
Filippo A. E. Nuccio has marked this topic as resolved.

Anatole Dedecker said:

This makes me a bit sad because I find these explicit parameters are just clutter when writing the code,

I think there's some elaboration magic that goes on here than means you can write hx.foo even though the signature is foo x hx
But the goal view will show X.Cond.foo x ..., which while not hiding x is also not using dot notation
Something that's been suggested in the past is a delaborstor generator that would produce (... : x.Cond).foo
Eric Wieser has marked this topic as unresolved.
Wouldn't you need to write hx.foo x not just hx.foo?

No, for example:

def Nat.IsThree (x : Nat) : Prop := x = 3
def Nat.IsThree.three (x : Nat) (hx : x.IsThree) : Nat := 3

variable (h : Nat.IsThree 3)
#check h.three
(#new members > dot-notation skips explicit parameters @ 💬)

Ah, I see what you mean. But this example fails when it's a function:

def Nat.IsThree (x : Nat) : Prop := x = 3
def Nat.IsThree.three (x : Nat) (hx : x.IsThree) (y : Nat) : Nat := 3

variable (h : Nat.IsThree 3)
#check h.three 3 -- Nat -> Nat

I think Anatole was talking about docs#Submodule.IsCompl.projection and making the submodules p and q explicit, then it would still require you to do hpq.projection p q to actually use it as a function (hence the clutter when writing the code).
But I agree that's a good argument against this pattern
